extracted.intended_audience: writers (novelists, aspiring comic-novelists, self-published authors) and comedy writers moving into prose
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for adding comedy to novels or writing fully comic novels, aimed at authors (especially those transitioning from TV/radio/comedy). Covers craft, character, tone, marketing, and professional mindset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish funny novels vs genre novels with humor
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of comedy in books: a 'funny novel' (e.g., Bridget Jones, P.G. Wodehouse) whose primary purpose is to make you laugh, and genre novels that add humour to their primary genre (e.g., Richard Osman murder mysteries, Sophie Kinsella romances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide early whether you are writing comedy as the main genre or adding comedic tone to another genre, because this affects cover, marketing, pacing and expectations. Example: match cover branding to the primary genre while conveying humour subtly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four story fundamentals apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Every story needs a character (or two), a goal, obstacles in the way of that goal, and the world they inhabit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four elements as the base for comedy as you would drama; humour is layered on top of standard story structure rather than replacing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build characters who lack self-awareness ('cringe corner')
rubrics_metrics.description: Funny characters often lack self-awareness; identify the 'cringe corner'—things about yourself or characters that are ridiculous and revealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine personal foibles, grudges, irritations, and small embarrassments as material. Create situations that expose those flaws. Anti-pattern: making characters simply caricatures without believable inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy characters generally don't learn
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike drama where protagonists change, in comedy characters often return to their original flaws and make the same mistakes (sitcom characters 'never learn').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition and running gags to generate humour across scenes/chapters. Scoring note: comedic consistency can be more valuable than character growth in sustaining laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The antagonist is often the protagonist (internal obstacles)
rubrics_metrics.description: In comedy the biggest enemy is often the character's own flaw; their lack of self-awareness provides the main obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place internal flaws at the centre of plot complications. Craft obstacles that arise from who the character is rather than only external forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overwriting; cut ruthlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving from short/script writing to novel-length, writers tend to overwrite—adding needless description and purple prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continually 'cut, cut, cut.' Keep prose economical, remove excess adjectives, and maintain comic timing by trimming. Anti-pattern: luxuriating in detail that kills pace and jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: You don't have to be funny all the time
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel need not be laugh-a-page; constant attempts at humour will fatigue readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast—moments of seriousness or normalcy—to make humour land more effectively. Treat humour as seasoning, not constant background noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clichés are useful starting points; subvert by placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichés are shortcuts to truth and good as starting points; the trick is where and how you put them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar archetypes (fish-out-of-water, bad manager) but place characters in fresh situations or filter through strong character voice to avoid stale comedy. Anti-pattern: leaning on clichés without adding a new angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find your 'funny' and 'know thyself'
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand your individual sense of humour and where your strengths/weaknesses lie; 'know thyself' helps you find the comedic voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about what irritates you, what you find absurd, and write from that place. Develop voice through repeated practice and experimentation rather than forcing mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to lie — don't be forced to write only autobiographically
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'write what you know' is common advice, writers should also give themselves permission to invent and 'lie' in service of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your first novel is overly autobiographical and emotionally charged, consider writing something else first to gain perspective. Use autobiographical elements selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every joke is a momentary removal of sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often works by briefly withdrawing reader sympathy (e.g., character pratfalls, exposed flaws) so you can laugh and then reassume sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes that let readers laugh at characters while still feeling for them overall. Balance ridicule with empathy to avoid alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create new variations on running mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy benefits from repeated structural setups (running gags) where the character repeats failures in fresh ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find new ways to put the same character flaw into different predicaments so repetition becomes a source of escalating humour rather than boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt timing/delivery for prose (no crowd feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike stand-up, novels lack live audience feedback and timing cues; writers must craft beats on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentence rhythm, paragraph breaks, dialogue beats, and pacing to reproduce comic timing. Test with readers to gauge what lands without an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice with sketches and short forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Write short self-contained sketches (2–3 minutes) to practice comic structure; 'sketches are to sitcom what the short story is to the novel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sketches to hone character, punchlines, twist endings, and tight economy. Transfer those techniques into longer fiction in small, controlled chunks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of joke-writing vs novel word count
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes can be very short; a novel requires sustained material, so balance concise joke mechanics with longer narrative needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to string short jokes into long stretches; scaffold comedic beats within scenes and chapters and use editing to preserve sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cover and branding to signal humour while matching genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers should convey that a book is humorous but must also fit primary genre conventions so readers find it in the right place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your book is a murder mystery with humour, lean on murder-mystery cover tropes while adding comedic signals (type treatment, copy). Poor alignment risks confusing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome fear of offence; develop a thick skin
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often fear negative reactions ('cancel culture'), but indifference (nobody noticing) is a more common and serious outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that humour is subjective; some will love it and some won't. Publish, learn from feedback, and if self-published you can revise quickly. Anti-pattern: withholding work out of fear of a minority reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publishing enables quick revision for dated/offensive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-publishing lets authors update text quickly if language later proves problematic or dated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor reader response and cultural shifts; make edits when warranted rather than avoiding publication altogether. Example: revise questionable lines within days rather than waiting months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking and submitting to topical outlets creates opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: For comedy careers (TV/radio), learning to write topical jokes and networking with producers opens doors; daily shows need material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop topical writing skills, seek credits on shows, and build relationships with producers and peers in your humour niche. For books, connect with the self-publishing community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a growth mindset; write to get better
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on improving craft rather than immediate success; writing because you want to become a better writer sustains long-term progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan long-term, practice regularly (short stories, sketches), and treat each project as experience. Avoid trying to write 'the great comic novel' on the first try.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting with your most emotionally charged autobiographical material
rubrics_metrics.description: First novels often default to the author's own story, which can cause emotional attachment and limit perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider writing a different project first so you are less emotionally invested and more able to shape story and humour objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast and restraint for better comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour lands more effectively when contrasted with normal or serious moments; restraint prevents over-saturation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically place jokes and let scenes breathe. Anti-pattern: relentless jokiness that numbs reader response.
